blocks.x: You ready? Let's see. The first thing I'd like to get is your name. I'm Bernd Stratus. And let's see, we're recording today. It's September the 22nd, 1960. We're aboard the steamer president. And we're Dr. Ede Splasser. That's right. Right at the foot of Canal Street. This is real one.
I'm Paul Crawford.
Let's get the Stratus family straight. There's so many of you. I know there's so many of you in the riverboat family that captains aboard the various boats.
What do you mean, the brothers that are in the business?
Yes.

Well, that was Joe, which is the oldest. And Roy's second, John third, and then on fourth. And H. Was your father? Father started the business in 1895. And built the first excursion boat that was used exclusively for one-day excursions, the steamer JS, built in 1903. And at that time, it was run on the upper Mississippi River and came to New Orleans and ran harbor trips for the first time in 1903.

And you personally, how long have you been aboard these boats? Ever since I was out of school. Ever since I was out of school. Of course, while I was in school, I was on them each summer. I made the summers on the boats. Do you mind if I ask your exact age? 65. And what is your birthday? July 27th. July 27th. So that would make you go on in 1895. 1895. 1895. See? And so you probably remember back from almost the very beginning yourself. First time. And his first time, yes. When these boats started, did they have any music at all on them? Always had music. Always had an orchestra. Who was the first orchestra?

Well, the first orchestra, we had a piano player and two pieces, three piece orchestra. He was a colored piano player, Charlie Mills, who we thought at that time was the finest piano player in the business. In later years, he went to foreign countries and he played a command performance before he came to England. Later returned to Chicago and very comfortably. He was born and raised in Quincy, Illinois. And when he died, which was about four or five years ago, he was returned to Quincy with honors as being an outstanding citizen.

How many of your family are musical themselves? Well, we all play the instruments a little bit. Two brothers played the piano and two played the violin. Which two played the piano? Joe and John, and Roy and I played the violin. I see. So you know how to listen carefully to the music and judge the talent. Oh, we like music, yes. Who was playing with Charlie Mills? Do you remember the other two songs? The first name I don't know. That was the combination of piano, violin and drums. That was the first combination. And later on, of course, went to the larger one.
And then, I was a band of drums.
How long was Melton on the band?

The violin player? The violin player, yeah. The violin player was Charlie Hershoff from Dora, Illinois. And the drummer was, the name was Little. The first name I don't know. That was the three, that was the combination of piano, violin and drums. That was the first combination. And later on, of course, went to the larger orchestras. How long was Melton on the band? And then he broke in another piano player by the name of Fate Merrill, Fate Merrill from Patooga, Kentucky, to play the clap. His fellow Charlie Mills was the best clapboard player we ever had. He was the original. We had clapboard those days. He broke in Fate Merrill who played the clap. This was done on the trips down the river and would stop between towns and then he practiced in two or three hours. He was a little disturbed the public. I guess that would wake a whole town up. Well, this fellow Fate Merrill then became a very fine piano player and always had the orchestra on the boat and then on and worked with all the rest of his life. He had the orchestra in New Orleans called the Cotton Fingers. He played in New Orleans here mostly in the heyday. It was around 1920. And he was the first fellow to employ William Armstrong. Fate Merrill with him.
Now. D-
But the excursion boats had the 8-9 piece bands, which we still have now.
The JS then was your first one and that stayed on for a long time? 1903 until 1910.

1910, I know. And then what boat came? Well then the boat all of a sudden succeeded her and she ran from 1910 to 1920. And she was succeeded by the steamer capital from 1920 to 1933. And then this boat came and took over 1933.
And what were the smaller boats?
Well we had boats called the Quincy, the St. Paul, the Sidney, and the Butte. We had four wood boats that time.
And do you remember any of the orchestras that played on those boats?
Not too well. They were orchestras that would just come for the summer months for four or five months in the summertime. And they would only operate for the summer months. I don't remember that.
You don't remember, say, Ed Allen's Golden Leaf orchestra?

Well we had a man by the name of Allen from Algears who played on the Capitol. They were on New York. He played on the Capitol every once. He was a player. Red Allen. Red Allen was a player. He played in the Big Marbles band. Red Allen.
Oh yes. Well I've heard him in person. Do you remember some of the other outstanding musicians who played with Fade on, say, the Sidney back in that era? Well there were several good musicians.

One was the Dodds, the drummer, who was a very good drummer and traveled extensively and better bands. Later on I had a band, a family band. And the bass player is still playing in one of the bands in Chicago now. I don't remember his name. He couldn't read music at that time. But he was a very good bass player anyhow. One of the best colored bands in the business.
Let's see. Do you remember a fellow named David Jones? Yes, he was a Sullivan player.
It wasn't a Sullivan player, but a mellophone player.
I know, I think that... It's either Louis Armstrong or Baby Dodds that talks about him and has such a beautiful tone.
That's right. He played on the boat at the time that Louis Armstrong played. He was a mellophone player. I've known the instrument. We haven't had one since.
What did the people like to dance to in those times, in the Sydneys times, before you ever had the capital?

Well, they liked the regular straight music, the pox files and waltzes. One one steps of course, and that's what they call him in the early days, and that's what they mostly do. Most of the band played. Just great music. And of course, some of the fancy steps came along, but some of the youngsters played for a while, dance for a while. But our business is built upon a really straight music. Written music. That's right. All, uh, not arranged, strictly, uh, music from the publisher. Music from what? From the publisher, not arranged music.
Oh yes, I see.
The band played music as it was published, not distorted by arrangements. They would, uh, take just a stop. Stock arrangements.
Not fancy it up or anything. And, uh, then when the capital came in, along in that era, did you see any changes in the dance system? No, it, uh, stayed the same.

And, uh, we find that, uh, in our business today, why, that the people that come aboard the booth, uh, still like straight music the best. If you watch, uh, the people dance, the ones with the fathom and the rumblings and all the rest of them come along, they all walk off, and then the, uh, pretty music comes on, and even the waltz, why they'll, uh, come and kill the floor again. They still, the patrons that we have still like good dance for music. Pretty music. But good rhythm. Must have good rhythm. See? Well now, did any of the musicians play by ear?

Well, most of them, Louie Armstrong played by ear. When he came with us, he couldn't read a note. And if he still doesn't, I don't know if he reads yet or not, but he didn't read music when, uh, came with us. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Would he play a little variation softly or would he get up and be featured?

Not at first. He didn't know he was very bashful. In fact, he never played for a white person before he played on the Capitol. He was playing in the Economy Hall with Oliver Norris at the time. We knew him and we went down to hear him and he was so outstanding. We tried to hire him but he wasn't on board the board on the town playing with white people. So we had Will get him. And he didn't have a cornet or he just known as a cornet. So we had a cornet on the boat and we loaned it to him. He played with us for a year and more with our cornet. He didn't have one. But that was the first time we ever played for public outside of the Pluttered Hall was on the boat. But he never featured himself. In fact, he never stood up and took a solo until one night. My brother remembers it at the Brothersville, Missouri. He had some dreamy pieces to play and they turned the lights low and he told them to go take the cornet down by himself. And he made such a big hit that from then on he was just elated and he wanted to do it more. But up until that time he didn't want to, he never wanted to stand up. He was always a very bashful fellow. What about Fate? Would Fate be featured? Oh yes, because he had the, he played the Plyopi and he also had the, an Organo poem that he made in Muscatine Highway. He would play, had the, were sitting right next to the panel with an air, a pair like they have with the days. Only one of the first ones. And some certain pieces he would play on the Organo poem. It was in staccato tempo and they had the, give the dancers just what they wanted. The pieces that he played on the Organo poem were just tops. And he wouldn't play too many of them even though. Just one of about every six pieces where he'd play on the Organo poem.
I don't think I've ever heard of an Organo poem.

Well it was made by the Tangley Manufacturing Company, Muscatine Highway. They still make them and they made them for the circuits and so on. Later on, instead of having the steam clavis going on down, they had the, what they call them in those days, the Organo poem. Now they have just the air clavis going on the column. We had that 30 years ago.
It was the same sort of sound as a calavis, I mean, sort of like that.

It had the, the effect of a clavis. It was a soft note, pretty note, but by making the staccato, you'd put it, make it a staccato note. But it was on the soft side. But quite, uh, you could play the Organo poem and fill the hall without any other attachment or application. It was that loud, you know, if you wanted to. It was, uh, very worthwhile. That's one of the time and the features, you know. What did the power of the notes come from?
It was an air, air, air. What about the people like Steve Lewis and Jeff Stacy and those other piano players?

Well, we had them on the boat. We had, uh, in the early days, they played for a band, uh, Tony Catalano from Damport, Iowa. Had the best band in the part of the coming days. That was on the river. And he called the ponies, Iowans. And he had, uh, Stacy and the big spider back in the Georgia. And, uh, some very good men. But they traveled up and down the river. So we used to go from port to port in the summertime. And they would come to the water in the wintertime. And they would get off and the other band would take over during the winter months. But that's only, uh, two really outstanding men that, uh, they were in the wintertime.
We had any room or shorts. I guess there were all the good men, but they never went on to fame like Dix and that's days yet. That's right. That's too bad. So many good musicians never did get.

We had this fellow New Orleanser, Paul Mares, and, uh, this good trombone player. But, uh, the two of us in the family, a little bit of a fellow. He played on the JS one summer. They were playing at the, uh, Briars Inn in Chicago. And, uh, then they came over and joined our board at Evansville, Indiana and made the summer season with us. It was really a fine combination. They'd been together for several years. And, uh, there were two or three of the boys were playing the Royals here.
Do you remember, uh, Leon Rapolo, a clarinet player? That's the one I'm talking about. He was on the boat. He was on the boat. Oh, yes.
He made the summer on there one summer, way back in 19, in the 20s, I think, in the 28s, 20s, or 20s.

I saw Santopocor on here the night that, uh, Turk Murphy was here. And they had the, uh, Columbia recording people here. I think he was, huh? Santo, I know. He played with that band. And then there was a fellow called George Bernice that played trombone with him, too. He's from a musical family. I thought maybe you remember George.

Not too well. Of course, the kind of been on there by the while. He, uh, he wanted to just die a few years ago. He was a kind of Paris who lived there. He was a little bit of a, uh, color, color, color. Is that what I thought? Yeah, it's supposed to be the best team.

Well, let's see. Norman Basin is still alive. Johnny Dodge, Fountain Blue, Fountain Blue. No. It's just been, uh. Johnny Dodge, uh, Lorenzo. Could Lorenzo Tio have played on the boat? I'm trying to remember. No.

No, not Tio. Earl Fink. But, no. This man really won't be, uh. Is it that? Was it with Faye? Or with P-ron? No, he played with P-ron. He played with P-ron. Oh, okay. Well, I could find that, uh. Well, no, then, uh, that was on the color side. Now, on the white side, the, uh, the white color side a couple of years ago. He played with Earl Dan on there for a couple of years. Earl Dan had the band on for two or three years.
Oh, uh, Blue was on. Fasola, Fasola, yeah. Blue Pristotnik and Irving Fasola were both here.

Fasola was on for a couple of years. Yeah. Let's see. In fact, when he first came down, he replaced the kind of band. And I wondered why they even put him on. I didn't think he was that good. You didn't think Fasola was that good? No. He went out to get a boy, a regular boy was sick, and Dan had Fasola come down. We didn't like him too much. We didn't think he didn't fit in with the band very well. But later on, he was also really good. I don't want to develop, but I guess it was at the time we didn't realize him. But he was, you know, really good.
He certainly had a beautiful tone. Oh, yes.
Danton was his fellow's name. Earl Danton. He's still in town. My brother Lloyd plays the bass. Earl plays saxophone clarinet. He had the band in town. He's still . What do you know Earl Danton?
I remember .
I met Lloyd . Earl . He had the band . He's been a band for many years.
Gee, there's so many people I ask you about. It's odd to know where to stop. I'm trying to think. What about Piron was on the boat for a while. I can't remember who was in that band.

That must have been good. He had a good band. Piron had a good band. He used to go over this summer. He played Louisiana in the winter time and he lived on the boat in the summer. He had a good band. That's where the piano player has been at the old absent house now. It started with Piron. That's the absent house now.
Well, was this the same guy who was on here when the television people were here and played the Kalanke? Is that the one, Fats Pichon?
Fats Pichon started with Piron. He played with him for a few years. We always played with him in the summer. He was on the boat. He was on the boat.

He was on the boat. He was on the boat. He was on the boat. He was on the boat. What about Steve Lewis? When was he on the boat? I don't remember Steve Lewis. He was supposed to play the Kalanke here. I think in his... Put a raincoat on or something. Walk out of that water. Maybe they all did. Well, they could. But they always put cotton in the rear. They did that. Because it was pretty loud. You see, if you could play it louder. Except for the one of the steam pressure, they have a rain.

They'd foul them. If you wanted to carry a great distance and made it hard for the panel player to play it. So you only have 28 keys. And you know, they're not going to play the Clack. But they always put cotton in the rear. They did that. Because it was pretty loud. You see, if you could play it louder. Except for the one of the steam pressure, they have a rain. They foul them. If you wanted to carry a great distance and made it hard for the panel player to play it. That's why then you give them a little more an early. They foul. But very few people don't play the Clack. So you only have 28 keys. And everything has to be. Because now, the piano first, the first, We have a five-pound boat in St. Louis now in the afternoon. We play for the entertainer, the people in the afternoon. It's a big thing. And it happens with the piano player. It's an A1 piano player. He can call on right quick. In fact, we've had a five-pound number eight years. He took it off on the other boats in the afternoon. And he plays it in the afternoon. And the night fellow plays it at night, but the man at night is not nearly so good. But in the afternoon, he goes on a concert. It's really worthwhile. The boat carries 4,500 people. And everybody that can get on that top deck goes up there to listen to that five music. And those kids go home and talk about it until next year. And they want to go back to that five. It's something they never hear. Any other place like that. It's close to it and I don't see how it's done. Did you hear it in St. Louis?
No, I wish I had known about it.

Did you go on the Admiral? No, I was up there. I was up there. I was up to the band just for two weeks. And I was out of part of February and first part of January. What were you last year? This year. What's the place where you're at? The Jefferson. Jefferson. Jefferson. Yeah, okay. What was the list of bands? Not a minute. Half of them. Not a minute. Oh, I see. Last summer they had the new policy of changing bands every so often. They started off with a new woman that was in the pool of our room. Yeah, that's right. It's probably a little better than that. That's right.
It's not interesting to me that that talk about economy at all. Where did you go to find talent?

Well, fate would go around and get the talent and he said, see, we needed a good orchestra. But this Louis Armstrong, he was touted as being so good, you know, and how would you ever get to hear him unless you went around to hear him? And I remember I went down to hear him and that night they were sitting up in the balcony. Of course, you put the room in those days. You had to get a permit to go in because it wouldn't even walk around because it was so strict. And they were all sitting up there in their shirt sleeves and Oliver and Ori, of course, it was King Oliver and Ori with the brown belt and Oliver was playing with the one eye. And they were all up in their shirt sleeves and they were spiring and carrying on. But the, the manager heard Louis play away. We didn't have to stay there very long. They wanted him. So we hired him. He lived up on Rampart Street at that time. And we had to go up and get him out of the room to bring him to work for you. So, scared about coming down. What about white talent?
Would you go around to the night club?

No. No. No. The white artists have always just been used to do since I brought to all the talent. They never did. In the old days, we were much more interested in the band. But now we're just going seven nights a week. It was very important that we had a good band. The band rehearsed regularly. Even Bates band. We had the, Sharniowski come on and rehearse the band. The fellow who was a singer for so many years. We had a stage band. He was a singer. And he was a lesson. And he went out to the Chicago theater. He lived there for eight or ten years. The Chicago theater. But he was a perfectionist. And he would teach these fellows how to tune. The fellow fellows don't know how to tune their instruments. He knew how to tune them. He would come on before they'd ever start or pull it. He'd absolutely make sure that they'd tune properly. And we didn't want him to change the style of the music that the fellows were playing. Only to, on certain pieces, have a little more grace to them. And also that, on waltzes and so on, they would have a little class to them. And then he, he did do that for them. And they would practice three or four times a week. And it was low with it because they did have a good band. In fact, he went along the river and they thought it was the best band. And he had a little talent along the river. Well, they never heard anything like it. Big Maribona's top period.
What about Dewey Jackson? Do you remember him? Yeah, he played on the road.

He played on the St. Paul for years. He's now a porter up to Jeltson, I guess. He might have someone up there. He had been. I think he was working somewhere else. He just plays, he plays now a spot job. Pretty good partner player. He's come aboard, bring a band. He's been a band once in a while after a big Maribona. He's gone one or two seasons. And then, uh, Dewey Jackson came down with a band from St. Louis. But a good corner player himself, but, uh, not such a good organiser. But we had the best color band from St. Louis, and it used to be on the list of St. Louis, called Charlie Clip. He was the best. He was a cornet player, and he had rhythm, and, uh, he would have a very fine band. He would compete with any band in the city. We had Charlie Clip in the summertime. Charlie Clip in the summertime. He had two boys operating in St. Louis in the summertime. Charlie Clip in the summertime. Charlie Clip in the summertime. We'd hire a white band in the summertime. We had, uh, Jules Bufino, who'd come down for the summer months on his DS. It was very deluxe boat. And, uh, he's now playing, you know, with, uh, Jimmy Moratti. And he had a band at that time. And, uh, we had Ralph Williams from Chicago. He had a little bit of a nice band. He's still in New Venice now. In Chicago. So we used to hire a band out of Chicago every summer for, uh, the three months we operated this deluxe boat, uh, newbie white. They had the color band in, uh, cheaper boat. They had the white band on the deluxe boat. How much would it cost to get in the deluxe boat? Well, it, it, it was, uh, McDonald's border up. And, uh, this boat, uh, it was a JS power, however. It was a very pretty boat. And, uh, he's run days during the night. And then we would, uh, we'd serve meals. Very good meals on the boat. And it was really considered the place to go. And, uh, we even had the, uh, the best piano player on a certain night, which the leading, the prominent lady that had, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the prominent lady that had, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the care of all the day before the party, she would have a trip on the boat on Friday night. And she would have this, uh, down a pair. I kind of remember now. He would come down and, uh, play on that particular night just to keep thinking of, uh, high-class man, you know.
That's in St. Louis. That was in St. Louis.
I had the white piano on. Yes.
Do you remember a colored piano player called, uh, Loving Good?

He wants to come down here and play the clap before us, or play, uh, right now on the board. He lives in Washington, D.C. And I heard from the other day. Called him over long distance phone. And, uh, yes.
See, we were talking about Jay Barr's Loving Good. That's right. He's in Washington, D.C. now. He had previously lived in, uh, California.

And, uh, I just remember the other night that Captain Roy told me on the phone that he'd called him long distance phone and, uh, just wanted to talk to him again. Just had the urge of talking to someone he'd worked for many years ago, you know. He was, uh, and, uh, he was the extra piano player. We had, uh, at one time, twin pianists. And, uh, Fate and I would play on, uh, one-handed band, uh, and Leving Good the other. They were different types of piano players. Leving Good was, uh, more, uh, uh, up and down keyboard, and Fate was more for rhythm. So we had twin, uh, really, uh, kind of what we called introduced twin pianos in those days. Now, of course, it's common all the time. The piano bars have three years and so on, but we had it many years ago.
I guess many people had it then. I can't think of any bands that were featured. No, they didn't have it.

When we had it the first time, and, uh, it was just an idea. We thought this fella came along and he was so good, it, uh, we didn't want to replace Fate, so we just put two of them on. So we had, uh, double cameras. Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .

Captain Vern's breakfast, Reel 2, September the 22nd, 1960. All right, so we're talking about people, uh, from across the room. Do you remember, by the way, do you remember Baby Dodge's brother Johnny who played clarinet?
Yes, he was on the boat too, I remember, the clarinet's parents.
Was he a reader?

Yes, I believe that, uh, they were a little later than the original fellas, and then they began to read. I think Maribor could read because he was, his mother was a pianist, he was the Duke of Kentucky. That's why he could lead a band of colored fellas that, uh, in other words, he could read the music. That's why he loved. The men didn't have to read the, he could play it through on the piano first, and they could digest it from there on. But the rest of the men didn't read very good. They put the music up in front of them, but that's all the good he did there. They changed me just as religiously as they could be, but it couldn't be any.
Do you remember Carlisle Evans?

Carlisle Evans, yes, he was out of Davenport, Iowa. He played on the boat with Tony Catalano. He was the piano player with Tony Catalano at one time, and he succeeded, uh, Stacy, I believe, Carlisle Evans. They wanted to have a band of his own for a few years.
Fred Fleck was the name of the band. I'm not sure. I don't remember his name.
I don't remember his name.
It's hard for me to keep all these names straight.
I don't remember so many names, but I remember Carlisle Evans because he was a piano player. He was a good one.
What about Nat's story? Do you remember him?
Yes, he's, uh, he was a trombone player. And a good one, and he's now in Purdue, Kentucky, and he's, uh, teaching trombone in one of the schools. Nathaniel Storyans.
And who did he play with?
He played with Peyton Marlowe.
He'd been on the boats, but I didn't know when.
He played with Peyton Marlowe.
That'd be early or late years?

Early, early years. He, uh, well, he'd be, I forget the guess of what years it would happen, but, uh, he would, Peyton Marlowe, and there's a whole length of time we were in the honors for 20, 25 years, and so, these are fellas coming different times, but, uh, he was one, uh, he was there for three or four years. He always wanted to put a band on the boat, but we never just let him put one on, but, uh, he was a good man. He was a trombone player.
Norman Mason, we mentioned, as being around St. Louis, I think he played with two or three of the different bands. He played saxophone, ball, ball, ball, ball.
He played saxophone. Norman Mason played saxophone.
He did play cornet at one time.
Yeah, he played cornet at one time. I don't remember when. I saw cornet at one time. Did you?
He was good for you.
Yeah, right? Yeah. Oh, wow. I haven't seen him here. He looks very strong and healthy. He's looking as a pleasant color. Uh-huh, he's alright. He's a good color on here.
What about the recordings of these bands? Did that have anything to do with the boat at all when they made the records?

Well, none of them recorded while they were on the boat. In fact, in the early days, amplification, you know, was in the infancy. I mean, our first application, I know we just had a battery out at Western Electric, however. In fact, we had the first application, I think, on any dance hall in the city. And it was a Western Electric job, and it was all battery. And then later on, they came with another model that was half battery and half power for part of the current. So we had the horns and the trumpet type horns. They didn't use the type we use now. And there were trumpet type horns right at the corner of the bandstand.
I guess they used megaphones too at some point.

Well, we had, from 1920 on, we had amplification. We knew that we needed it for the, the capitals bandstand was right in the middle of the hall, like this one that's here. And when it became crowded, by the end, it wouldn't get any music. So we had to do something. So the first thing that came out, the way of amplification, and of course, they had a big kind of a microphone. I had a big round microphone before. They were all the Western Electric job. And they've since gone out of the business. They don't even, they don't even make it anymore. But they were the only ones that made amplification in those days as any consequence. They were the only people living in the business.
One thing you're talking about rhythm, what did you demand of a drummer on the boat? I know that's very important.

Well, we didn't have to say about it except that he should be heard to a certain extent. It was very important that the people at the hearings, like the Lawrence Welk Band, if you notice his recordings, every one of them has a little drums to it. I listened to one last night and there's always a little bit of drums coming through. Sometimes people say they shouldn't hear too much drums, but if they don't hear the beat, they just can't dance. That's all there's to it. Even if the music is good. Of course, the bass player, he's in there too. He's very important. And the piano player with a good left-hander is very important too. So many of them don't have it.
So you watch them pretty carefully?

We used to. We don't anymore. We don't ever sing the band anymore. We haven't talked to the band in years. We let the leader take care of it. It seems a bit different. It's a big difference now from what I've given before. So they couldn't do what they wanted to, but if they don't produce a good band, you just don't have them back anymore. Right now though, I know it's the record now, but I think people are the best playing band.
I think the kind of band, I think it's good too for the dance band. Oh, it's pretty good.

Have you heard Gito's bands even on the board? Well, it's a very full band. We've had every band in the city and I don't think we've missed any. We've had them all on special occasions. We've had them for some time, about a month and so on. And this band is a full band. And it has pretty good rhythm. And some of the people say we're too slow, some of the real slow drives, we're just a little bit too slow. But we haven't seen anything about it. It takes a lot of let it go along for a while. Just make sure that maybe he's right and we're wrong. But he has a good band. He's got a good sax session. Oh, a good sax session. And good trombone player too. And a good cornet player. Yeah, he is. You thought he was good. That's why Mick Lala is a good cornet player. He follows his father's footsteps and his fine shape. He's father played on Airbusphere for four years. And we thought he was very good. In fact, we wanted to organize a band one time, but he didn't want to go up to his tent and everything. He was getting all that music together. 60 or 70 numbers. And I taste my library and all. And Airbus is going to pool with it. He didn't like the man either. But he certainly looked good. Well, you say the piano player is good too. The piano player is very good.
He's got quite a teaching band. You know, he's got three teachers in the band. You teach two? No. The lead sax man is a history teacher. The middle fellow.
The name.
The ball of his. Yeah. The piano player teaches in public schools music. And the third sax is a music teacher too. Is that right?

I didn't know the piano player I taught to you too. But he is good. I mean, and he seems to love to play the piano. I mean, some people enjoy their nice work. And he just seems to enjoy the Indians work. He's a good. Although the music is good, I think all the musicians like it. It's only when everybody's out of step and people don't like it. The rhythm is bad. They have a lot of blue notes so I, it goes against the grain. But I find the band, with all due respect, as you know, there's good men in the band. And some of the Reims are very, very classy. When he modulates from one to the other, it's clever. It's just like Dan Garber or any good orchestra, Guy LaVarro, or any of you. He sounds like them. It has the same effect. I went home the other night and played Dan Garber's record. His last one out, it was Nidalee's. You know, to just see how it compares to the band having the booth. Tell them, I thought our band was better than he did. Sounds better than he did on the record. I really thought so.
So you haven't catered to rock and roll, or you don't try for any of those changes that have come back.

No, the band's private, and then we've had rock and roll bands on the booth. And it's good for just one time. But not good for business. And that's the younger generation, and there are kids that you really don't want to cater to that type of place. We'd rather have the middle-aged people, or just in their twenties, you know. These kids, we'd rather not have them on the booth. And so we never did cater to it. Our business has always been built up on really straight music. And it never did try it, because you can try a few numbers and you'll get a little long for it and so on, but then they don't come back anymore. It drives other people away. They do too much throwing out and too much hitting and so on. And they make some uncomfortable other people to dance, they just, they won't go on the floor and dance. It's much better to have, you have to have one or the other and have to make up your mind. We like the straight dancing. And they can go to the little night clubs around town and do the other if they like.
You know, Fate did make one record, by the way.
He did? I didn't know that.
Oh, okay. It's in the public library here. You could go hear it.
Is that right? I didn't know that.
Keanu, Flage, and Frankie and Johnny. That's right. And he had Pops Foster and Zutty Singleton on drums. Uh-huh. Two Cornets, Amos White and Sidney Deadzvins.
I believe Norman Basin's on it too. Uh-huh.
And Dewey Jackson made a record called Capitol Blues that they put out. How about that? Which I guess is after the SS Capitol.
Uh-huh. Well affected. Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. Dewey played on the Capitol. But it was in the- after that the boat laid up. So I think it must have been in the map works. You must really follow music. He knows all the names of all the good men. Of your hobby with you, aren't you?
Oh, yes. Well, it's my job now.
You have to like it too with it, I guess.
Oh, yes. Well, I collected records for years and I studied trombone too. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. That kind of thing. It just gets in your blood, you know?
That's right.
Remember the names and different things like that. Let's see. Who else came off the boat that was outstanding? This saxophone player and carnet player used to be with Fat Swallow. Gene Cedric?
Yeah, Gene Cedric. Little Fat Follower. That's him.
Yeah. I saw him in New York about a year ago, a little over a year ago.
He was very good when he was on the boat.
Still playing. All right. Still going strong. Do you remember if he was with Fade or was that? Yes, he played with Fade. He was with Fade, not with him.
That's right. Fade with Fade. Eugene, Cedric.
Could you talk a little, ask a little about the crap.
I'd like to know more about the crap too.

Well Charlie Cedric was a cornet player and he specialized on rhythm. He really knew how to play the kind of music that the people wanted. He played on the St. Paul of St. Louis. He had, well the people, well the boat did a very nice business and was due to the fact that this fellow really put out, had the best music in town. He was a good boy and he handled his men in pretty good shape. Later years, he looked not pretty bad so he didn't play too much cornet, too much cornet, but he would always get a good cornet player with him. And on the good pieces that he really wanted to stand out on, he would take it down and that seemed to satisfy the people and they still came to hear Charlie Cedric. And he later left us and he went to Chicago and finally dropped out of the music and put his back there all together. But when he was in his heyday, he was a good cornet player and had as good a band as he did once.
But would he play the blues on the boat and all?
Oh yes, he played it. He rocked them and everything, but not in the style we call rock and roll now. He made them swing. It was real good music, good danceable music.
Do you remember any mutes that either he or Dewey Jackson would use?

Not particularly. They didn't use this too much. In fact, Dewey Jackson played much too loud. He was a loud type and featured himself a great deal. And that was one of the drawbacks. He did play pretty loud, Dewey Jackson did.
I think of that drum. Floyd Campbell, I guess his name was. He sang and played drums, I think with Dewey. Maybe he played with the Press, too.
Could have been. I think I remember the name.
He sang. He made one record where he sang and the band backed him up. Back to Press. Did they ever have a violin on those bands?
No, only one P-Round was on the boat.
It was the only time. That's right.

And in the early days when they had this orchestra on the J.S. From the little Charlie Herzog. He played the violin in the early days. Otherwise, not much on the violin. You couldn't hear it for one thing. And if you played the band, they were soft enough that you could hear the violin. And they couldn't dance to it. That was before amplification. And then, played it on, but I just never really get back to violin.

The Press made one record where it's guitar player Lonnie Johnson played violin. I don't remember that. Dead sure. That's funny. I can't remember the people who played the track. I just haven't thought about it for a while.
I don't think they were outstanding to an extent that he just trained them and they were good for him, but they weren't good for anybody else. I don't know.
Was there a drummer called Mousy? Or maybe it's a trumpet player called Mousy. I'm confused. Irving Randolph is called Mousy. He's a trumpet player.
He never played on the boat, I don't think.

I don't know. There's so many people that are coming to me now that I want to look up. You know, there's a good many books about this that mention the band. Osceola Blanchett was a piano player too, I think. One of the books. It's hard to keep them all straight. I wanted to ask you about how your plans for the year would go. What you would do in the different poets. How did that work?

Well, we just stopped at Easttown one day, like a circus. We'd go to the next town. We'd operate on the upper Mississippi River and the upper Ohio. And go as far as St. Paul on the Mississippi and as far as Pittsburgh on the Ohio. And do that in the summertime. When we got to the terminus, like at St. Paul, we'd stay there about 10 days. Bigger town, Minneapolis, Paul. A million people would be in the two towns. And Pittsburgh is around 600, 700,000. So we'd stay there a longer time. But other towns would just stay one or two days at the most. I would make the same territory over and over all summer long by just going one town the other. It would be about 30 miles apart from town town. And all over 30,000 population in those days. And now they're going across about twice that size. So we would go from town to town day by day and run a day shirt and a night shirt. And go up the next town and do the same thing.
Did you advertise by posters in advance?

Oh, yes. Oh, yes. We had advertised by posters and newspapers. And organizations, too. We'd handle the best organizations in all the towns. It's sponsored mostly for day trips. In fact, we'd have the Teachers College of Wino in Minnesota. And, well, in fact, all the schools in the springtime, we'd get them in the towns. And others would be sponsored by women's organizations mostly. Church organizations and so on. They would go from one town to another during the day and come back and then we'd take the moonlight, which didn't stop any of us. Where would you spend your one? New Orleans, yeah. Always had a boat in New Orleans. The last 57 years, always had a boat here.
And would that boat stay here all the winter?

No. Years ago, it used to go away because there was no summer business there, you know. Tourists wouldn't come. There was no roads in Louisiana. So, if you came along and built roads by, you couldn't only come to New Orleans by rail. And they had to attend upon us strictly upon tourists. Well, tourists didn't come to New Orleans in the hot season. So, consequently, there'd be no business here in the summertime. So, we would go on the upper river where the business was and come down here in the winter pass. But, later on, why has changed? There was good roads and the vacations coming on with all the people having attended vacations. The summer business now has got to be equal to the winter business. So, we just stayed here to get around. And then, another thing, during the war, we had trouble with fuel. We couldn't get, we burnt fuel oil and we had to, all these towns had to have fuel ahead of us, you know. And we got into a place where we couldn't possibly get it. So, we had to, that was the reason for not going away in the first place. But then, after we stayed here, we found out it was alright to stay here. So, now we stayed here around. Since 1944.
Well, before 1944, what months would consist of the winter months for you?
Well, we'd come back in September and stay until May.
Quite a long season to stay in. Oh, yes.
We'd only go about three and a half months.
I always thought the family was from St. Louis and would spend a lot of time here.

No, Roy and I have lived here frankly all our lives. I did ever since we started running the bullshitter of the year round. I had two brothers in St. Louis, so we had a boy to St. Louis. And, uh, so Roy and I live in New Orleans and down in Joe lives in St. Louis.
Yeah, I'm running out of questions and people. And the call has some...
Oh, I'm just enjoying sitting here with it. What do you want to credit? Yeah, I think we... Or we can come back to see you again sometime. Oh, I find. Some cameras. Oh, I see sure.
See if there's, uh, anything of any other colors that we haven't thought about. Well, some of them...

segments.title: Opening and recording setup aboard the steamer President
segments.summary: Paul Crawford states the date, September 22, 1960, and the location at the foot of Canal Street.

segments.title: The Streckfus brothers, the family business and the first boat's trio
segments.summary: Verne names his brothers, his father's 1895 start and the 1903 steamer J.S.; the first orchestra was pianist Charlie Mills's three-piece group.

segments.title: Musical talents in the family and the first combination
segments.summary: The brothers play piano and violin; the first combination was piano, violin and drums.

segments.title: Fate Marable learns calliope from Charlie Mills
segments.summary: Charlie Mills trains Fate Marable, who leads the New Orleans boat orchestra around 1920 and first employs Armstrong.

segments.title: The succession of Streckfus boats from the J.S. to the President
segments.summary: Boats run J.S. 1903-10, then a successor to 1920, Capitol 1920-33, then this boat; smaller wooden boats also named.

segments.chapter: Fate Marable, Armstrong and the early bands
segments.title: Orchestras and sidemen on the smaller boats: Allen, Dodds, David Jones
segments.summary: Verne recalls little of the summer-only orchestras but names Red Allen, a Dodds drummer and mellophone player David Jones.

segments.chapter: Fate Marable, Armstrong and the early bands
segments.title: Straight published music for dancers
segments.summary: The boats played stock published arrangements, and patrons still prefer pretty straight dance music with good rhythm.

segments.chapter: Fate Marable, Armstrong and the early bands
segments.title: Louis Armstrong on the boat: bashful, reading by ear, first solo
segments.summary: Armstrong could not read music, was bashful, played on a loaned cornet and took his first solo at a dim-lit number in Brownsville.

segments.chapter: Fate Marable, Armstrong and the early bands
segments.title: The Organopoem on the Capitol
segments.summary: Verne explains the Organopoem built in Muscatine, used for staccato effect, and compares it to the calliope.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Tony Catalano's band and Stacy
segments.summary: Tony Catalano's Davenport band, with Stacy and Bix Beiderbecke, worked the river in summer.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Paul Mares, Rappolo and the Friars Inn band summer
segments.summary: Paul Mares's group from Friars Inn, with Leon Rappolo, joins the J.S. at Evansville for one summer; Crawford asks about George Brunies.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Earl Danton's band, Irving Fazola and Piron's players
segments.summary: Verne recalls Earl Danton's band and Fazola, whom he first doubted but later found good.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Piron's band and Fats Pichon on the boat
segments.summary: Piron's band summered on the boat; Fats Pichon started with Piron.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Calliope playing, and the afternoon calliope concerts in St. Louis
segments.summary: The calliope's loud sound and 28 keys, and the afternoon concert from the 4,500-passenger boat in St. Louis.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Scouting talent and hiring Louis Armstrong at Economy Hall
segments.summary: Fate Marable scouts talent; Verne goes to hear Armstrong with King Oliver's band and hires him.

segments.chapter: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
segments.title: Rehearsing the band: a perfectionist coach and tuning
segments.summary: Verne explains how the bands rehearsed regularly and a vocal coach taught them to tune.

segments.chapter: St. Louis bands and other players
segments.title: Dewey Jackson, Charlie Creath and white versus colored bands on St. Louis boats
segments.summary: Colored bands on the cheaper boat, white bands from Chicago on the deluxe boat, including Jules Buffano and Ralph Williams.

segments.chapter: St. Louis bands and other players
segments.title: Burroughs Lovingood and the twin pianos with Fate Marable
segments.summary: Verne recalls pianist Lovingood, now in Washington, and the twin pianos with Fate Marable.

segments.chapter: St. Louis bands and other players
segments.title: Players from Ed Allen's band, Pete Bocage and Algiers musicians
segments.summary: Crawford names Walter Thomas, Pop Foster and Emmanuel Perez; Verne recalls little but talks of Pete Bocage.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds and Fate Marable's ability to read music
segments.summary: Johnny Dodds was on the boat; Fate Marable read music and played parts through for the band.

segments.title: Carlisle Evans, pianist with Tony Catalano
segments.summary: Carlisle Evans succeeded Stacy with Catalano's band and led his own for a while.

segments.title: Nat Story, trombonist with Fate Marable
segments.summary: Nat Story played with Marable in the early years on the boats and now teaches trombone in Kentucky.

segments.title: Norman Mason, saxophone and cornet
segments.summary: Brief exchange about Norman Mason, who played saxophone and at one time cornet.

segments.title: Recordings and early amplification on the boats
segments.summary: No band recorded while on the boat; Western Electric amplification was installed from 1920 on the Capitol.

segments.title: What the boats wanted from drummers and rhythm
segments.summary: Verne wants the beat heard, with bass and piano left hand crucial; he now leaves band supervision to the leader.

segments.title: The current band on the boat
segments.summary: Verne and Speaker 3 discuss the present band's players and compare it to Jan Garber and Guy Lombardo.

segments.title: Rock and roll is not wanted on the boats
segments.summary: Verne explains the boats stick to straight dance music, not rock and roll.

segments.title: Fate Marable's record, Dewey Jackson's Capitol Blues, and Crawford's record collecting
segments.summary: Crawford says Marable made one record and Jackson recorded Capitol Blues; Crawford describes his hobby.

segments.title: Eugene Sedric on the boat with Fate Marable
segments.summary: Eugene Sedric played with Marable and is still going strong in New York.

segments.title: Charlie Creath's band on the St. Paul
segments.summary: Creath, a rhythm cornetist, led the St. Paul band to good business before leaving for Chicago.

segments.title: Dewey Jackson's loud style, mutes and Floyd Campbell
segments.summary: Dewey Jackson played loudly and used few mutes; Verne vaguely recalls Floyd Campbell.

segments.title: Violin in the boat bands
segments.summary: Only Piron had a violin; before amplification Charlie Herzog's violin could not be heard.

segments.title: Questions about Irving Randolph and Osceola Blanchett
segments.summary: Crawford asks about Randolph; Verne says he never played on the boat.

segments.title: The summer touring route and advertising
segments.summary: The boats toured the upper Mississippi and Ohio from town to town, with daytime and moonlight trips sponsored by organizations.

segments.title: Wintering in New Orleans and where the family lives
segments.summary: Boats left in summer until fuel shortages in the war led to staying in New Orleans year-round from 1944.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Crawford runs out of questions and they close with a hope to meet again.
